author: Codex socialist_green assessment agent (AI-assisted independent assessment)
changeNote: Completed 240 individually interpreted responses and separate substantive evidence review. User authorised neutral representative doctrinal modelling; no 12Axes answers or scores imported.

metadata.name: Marxism (classical Marx–Engels)
metadata.description: Classical Marx–Engels historical materialism and revolutionary workers’ politics, including transitional socialisation and the Commune interpretation.
metadata.scope: Classical historical materialism and revolutionary workers’ politics, including the Manifesto’s transitional programme and the later Commune interpretation. Later Leninist party-state doctrines are excluded. No incumbent government is treated as the direct embodiment of this historical doctrine. This is a representative interpretation, not a questionnaire submitted by adherents. Numeric neutral means a stated mixed/conditional judgement, including rejection of the premise where explained; it is not a claim of measured empirical equivalence. Modern biological and technology items are conditional interpretive judgements where no exact historical position exists; they must not be read as empirical findings or a representative survey of adherents.
metadata.phrase: A society overcoming capitalist class domination through workers’ emancipation and common control of production.

sources.title: Socialism, especially ownership, Marxist phases and human nature
Manifesto of the Communist Party, Chapter II (1848)
The Civil War in France, Third Address, III (1871)
Critique of the Gotha Programme, Part I (1875)
Socialism: Utopian and Scientific, Chapter III (1880)
Theses on Feuerbach (1845; Engels edited edition)
On the Question of Free Trade (9 January 1848)

axes.brief: Marx’s Commune model uses elected, recallable delegates and combines legislative and executive work; it is not liberal separation of powers.
axes.counterEvidence: Recall and universal suffrage counter an automatic autocratic reading. Marx also criticises judicial independence and liberal parliamentarism, so constitutional-liberal mechanisms are qualified.

answers.rationale: Elected and revocable delegates are essential, though national leadership need not follow a parliamentary contest model.
Hierarchical expert appointment contradicts the Commune’s suffrage principle.
Universal suffrage supports inclusion; applying it to all adults extends a historically male franchise.
Executive supremacy contradicts accountable collective workers’ rule.
Open working-class debate is valued but revolutionary class power does not guarantee equal standing to every restorationist party.
Revocable public servants should expose spending to scrutiny.
Marx proposes elected recallable judges rather than independent constitutional judicial supremacy.
Workers themselves should govern rather than a separate caste of union leaders.
Revolutionary defence may restrict counterrevolution, but personal ideological veto is not the Commune model.
Binding popular decisions fit producer self-government.
Rule by one national leader contradicts collective emancipation.
Recallable public office supports removing abusive leadership.
Leaders cannot suspend the accountability constitutive of workers’ power.
Immediate recall is explicit in the Commune account.
Public servants remain answerable to their constituents.
A separate military caste must not replace civilian workers’ authority.

axes.brief: Working-class emancipation opposes the old repressive machinery while allowing coercive protection of revolutionary change.
axes.counterEvidence: Acceptance of revolutionary coercion is not evidence for every surveillance or detention measure. Specific modern powers remain bounded inferences.

answers.rationale: Human emancipation supports autonomy while collective obligations qualify a purely self-regarding doctrine.
Serious-crime investigation may be necessary but inherited policing power is distrusted.
Collective working-class action requires protected public mobilisation.
Criticism is necessary for workers’ self-emancipation.
Social health can warrant collective measures but paternalistic command is not itself emancipatory.
Indiscriminate surveillance reproduces the repressive state machinery.
Preventing harm can justify checks while coercive policing remains suspect.
Revolutionary protection and resistance to arbitrary state power pull in different directions.
Free intellectual development opposes moralistic censorship.
Anonymous organising can protect collective action from repression.
Generalised suspicion enables class repression without individual grounds.
Actual danger may justify intervention but disorder is often used against workers.
Legal safeguards can limit coercion even if bourgeois courts are not final guardians.
Exposure of public misconduct supports accountable revocable officials.
The armed people and distrust of a separate military support civilian defensive capacity.
Unreviewed indefinite detention undermines accountable communal government.

axes.brief: International class solidarity resists national-cultural exclusion, but classical expectations of converging national differences are not modern multiculturalism.
axes.counterEvidence: Classical writings contain dated civilisational language and expect national differences to diminish. They cannot simply be read as a modern diversity charter.

answers.rationale: Common proletarian interests outweigh national cultural priority.
Equal participation supports practical accommodation within common institutions.
Workers need not adopt a dominant nationality’s customs.
Cross-national class membership can coexist with inherited identities.
Shared communication is useful, but exclusion through language undermines solidarity.
Recognition of dispossessed communities is consistent with opposing domination.
Predominant traditions deserve no automatic class-neutral claim on resources.
Sectional cultural identity should not outrank common emancipation automatically.
Coordination is necessary but a single cultural calendar is not inherently emancipatory.
A political community can include workers of several traditions.
Shared participation helps overcome divisions used against labour.
Practical language access supports common organisation.
National identity should not override international working-class solidarity.
Anti-clerical critique and opposition to coercive cultural exclusion do not select a categorical exemption.
Multiple ways of life are compatible with common social production.
Assimilation into inherited national customs is not a condition of emancipation.

axes.brief: Workers’ common interests support mobility and equal inclusion rather than employer or ethnic selection; institutional details are modern inferences.
axes.counterEvidence: No historical text settles modern sponsorship or graduate visa rules. Answers infer how class solidarity applies, not a documented administrative code.

answers.rationale: Class solidarity weighs against rigid numerical exclusion.
Workers should be able to seek better living conditions across borders.
Employer-usefulness tests subordinate people to capital’s requirements.
Family unity can be protected without a class-based admission filter.
Persecuted people should not be tested for cultural compatibility.
Opposition to exclusion supports regularisation, while no unconditional administrative rule follows.
Native labour cannot secure emancipation by excluding foreign workers.
Housing shortages require social production rather than an automatic migration response.
Family life should not be subordinated to a rigid quota.
A job offer generally supports movement, without making employer demand the sole criterion.
Workers’ freedom should not depend entirely on an employer or sponsor.
Education can establish connection but does not alone determine settlement terms.
Protection from persecution outweighs ordinary labour-admission caps.
National-cultural preference divides the working class.
Common social support should cover resident workers irrespective of origin.
Cultural difference itself is not the materialist criterion for admission.

axes.brief: Opposition to standing armies and class war coexists with armed popular defence and revolutionary force.
axes.counterEvidence: Armed revolution and the Commune militia are clear counter-evidence to absolute pacifism.

answers.rationale: National interest alone is not an emancipatory justification for force.
Peaceful settlement is preferable when compatible with workers’ emancipation.
Competitive standing armies reproduce class domination.
Defence against imminent attack is possible but revolutionary aims and evidence matter.
Legitimate revolution and anti-oppression conflict are not limited to responding to state attack.
A short citizen militia differs from a compulsory male national war apparatus.
Compromise can avert destructive wars without abandoning emancipation.
Unaccountable autonomous killing conflicts with popular responsibility for force.
A popular militia prioritises defence over standing-army campaigns.
Revolutionary and communal defence preclude avoiding all armed resistance.
A permanent expeditionary army contradicts the Commune model.
Territorial prestige is not sufficient reason to start a war.
Militarised national bargaining ordinarily serves ruling-class interests.
Preventing war generally outweighs displays of state power.
Intelligence may aid revolutionary defence but national rivalry alone is insufficient.
Negotiated arms reductions can weaken standing militarism.

axes.brief: International proletarian solidarity rejects national antagonism without endorsing every existing interstate authority.
axes.counterEvidence: Workers’ international organisation is different from allowing capitalist international courts or alliances unrestricted authority.

answers.rationale: National workers’ power is transitional, while international solidarity limits sovereign absolutism.
Workers’ international cooperation is supported, capitalist institutional command is not automatic.
Neither national nor international courts deserve priority regardless of class character.
Durable worker cooperation differs from binding military alliances between ruling classes.
Leaving oppressive interstate commitments may be necessary for emancipation.
Accountability is desirable but class-based international courts are not presumed impartial.
Proletarian solidarity outweighs national competitive advantage.
Common material conditions justify international environmental coordination.
Common policy can advance solidarity or bind workers to ruling-class blocs.
Universal emancipation supports rights but bourgeois international institutions are not unquestioned arbiters.
Monetary organisation depends on social control rather than national ownership alone.
Shared resources can support international emancipation and common needs.
Exclusive national border authority reinforces divisions within labour.
Shared rules help exchange but their class content remains decisive.

International working-class association is favoured, but national democratic institutions can remain during transformation; support depends on the proposed federation’s class character and accountability.
Collective action is justified by emancipation rather than enforcement of every interstate agreement.

axes.brief: The transitional Manifesto endorses state concentration of production; the Commune and Engels require real workers’ control rather than nominal nationalisation.
axes.counterEvidence: Engels explicitly says capitalist state ownership is not itself socialism. Government-ownership answers refer to the documented transitional workers’ government, not any state.

answers.rationale: Socialising production rejects a predominantly privately owned economy.
Utility networks fit transitional public control.
Equal service metrics do not remove exploitation under private ownership.
The Manifesto explicitly extends publicly owned factories.
Collective health provision should not normally rest on private productive ownership.
The Manifesto expressly centralises transport in public hands.
Cheaper contracting does not by itself justify restoring capitalist control.
A public bank is supported, although the Manifesto ultimately proposes a monopoly rather than coexistence.
Selling public production reverses the transitional programme.
Social control of land and shelter supports substantial public housing.
Regulation does not remove class control over strategic productive property.
Land and productive resources are to become common public means.
Routine capitalist contracting perpetuates private appropriation.
Strategic socialisation outweighs a one-off fiscal receipt.
Capitalist profitability is not the sole test of socially necessary production.
Public communications fit the programme if controlled by producers rather than an autonomous bureaucracy.

axes.brief: Marx’s 1848 speech conditionally prefers free trade for its revolutionary effect while denying that either capitalist trade system emancipates workers.
axes.counterEvidence: The speech’s support is tactical and historically conditional; no eternal commitment to unilateral free trade is inferred.

answers.rationale: Protection preserves bourgeois sectional interests rather than emancipating workers.
Marx conditionally favours free trade for its revolutionary historical effects.
Domestic capital deserves no automatic purchasing preference.
Open sourcing can develop production but capitalist freedom is not the ultimate objective.
Resilience may matter, while protective national capital is not inherently progressive.
Tactical support for openness does not establish every unilateral concession.
Infant-industry protection can develop capitalism but is not a socialist principle.
Foreign and domestic capital are equally subject to the intended socialisation.
The critique of Corn Laws weighs against protecting agricultural rents.
In the 1848 context openness exposes contradictions rather than insulating domestic capital.
Retaliation usually protects competing capitalist interests.
Nationality alone is no reason for differential product taxation.
Subsidies’ class and developmental effects matter more than their foreign source.
Wider exchange can advance production but dependence can reproduce domination.
Both domestic and foreign strategic capital are targets of social control.
International access to useful services is compatible with working-class solidarity.

axes.brief: Associated production and social planning replace capitalist market anarchy; transitional public instruments should answer to producers.
axes.counterEvidence: Common planning does not settle every modern price or currency instrument; transitional choices are qualified when worker participation matters.

answers.rationale: Social production should answer to associated producers rather than private firms.
Coordinated targets can implement a social production plan under worker control.
Market prices cease to be the principal coordinator as commodity production is overcome.
Public direction of investment implements the transitional programme.
Social need rather than solvent consumer demand should govern production.
Essential price controls can protect workers during transition.
Strategic production requires social coordination rather than unrestricted capitalist entry.
Centralised public credit is explicit in the Manifesto.
Unrestricted capital flight can undermine socialisation.
Directed resources can develop productive capacity before full social ownership.
Private currencies preserve competing private monetary power.
Legal wage floors can protect workers before wage labour is overcome.
Union negotiation helps under capitalism, while planned social production ultimately supersedes employer wages.
Public credit and monetary tools should support social planning.
Shelter should not be allocated solely by capitalist rental demand.
Coordinated production replaces the anarchy of independent capitalist output.

axes.brief: Progressive taxation and inheritance abolition are transitional measures; Gotha rejects making redistribution a substitute for changing production.
axes.counterEvidence: Gotha prioritises production relations and recognises unequal first-phase rewards. It does not promise identical individual income.

answers.rationale: Progressive fiscal measures support transition, though property relations remain primary.
The Manifesto explicitly legitimises graduated taxation.
Social funds should protect need during transition.
Common provision should exceed a minimal poor-relief floor.
Heavy progressive taxation is an explicit transitional measure.
Private retention cannot veto necessary social claims on production.
Abolition of inheritance is stronger than the question’s tax proposal.
Genuine need should not disappear from social responsibility after a fixed duration.
Wealth transfers can weaken concentrated property during transition.
Minimising social support for taxpayers conflicts with common provision.
Human development requires more than biological subsistence.
General tax cuts do not outrank workers’ material support.
Supplements can help but can also subsidise low wages without changing exploitation.
Flat marginal rates contradict the stated progressive tax measure.
Common land ownership is preferred; compensated individual redistribution is a conditional transition only.
Social funds should address broad developmental needs rather than destitution alone.

axes.brief: The Commune’s disestablishment, secular education and revocable civil offices strongly oppose clerical state power.
axes.counterEvidence: Critique of religion is distinct from a claim that people should be persecuted for private belief.

answers.rationale: Material social reasons rather than revelation should ground law.
Clerical doctrine should not have official legal authority.
Civil administration must be free of religious approval.
State religious foundations reproduce clerical privilege.
Secular education can critically study religion without cultivating belief.
The Commune removes religious control over public education.
Secular accountable institutions should make judicial rules.
Clerical review privileges an authority Marx seeks to disestablish.
Public administration should be separated from organised worship.
The Commune’s disendowment opposes public support for religious propagation.
State endorsement of a creed contradicts disestablishment.
Inherited holidays may remain socially, but official religious recognition is rejected.
Religious status must not confer public office.
Faith-specific fiscal privilege conflicts with disendowment.
Marriage should not require clerical authority.
Civil family relations should not be ruled by religious courts.

axes.brief: The Manifesto historicises family and morals and attacks women’s instrumentalisation, without providing a modern sexuality-policy checklist.
axes.counterEvidence: Historical sources do not directly answer same-sex marriage, modern identity terminology or abortion. Neutral applications express the tension between emancipatory transformation and refusal to specify a future moral code.

answers.rationale: Social institutions change with material relations and can be transformed deliberately.
Inherited tradition is not an overriding constraint on emancipation.
Critique of bourgeois family property supports recognition beyond its normative model.
Treating women as fixed instruments of production is explicitly rejected.
Emancipation challenges hierarchy, but classical family critique does not itself choose a modern marriage classification.
The bourgeois married household is not an eternal social ideal.
Freedom from domination and shared reproductive responsibility leave this modern ethical choice conditional.
Social education need not submit to inherited parental ideology.
Non-instrumental family relations support equality, but no definitive classical adoption model follows.
Historically contingent morals cannot bind all future public dress.
Language is socially changeable, but no universal identity-language rule follows from materialism.
Revolutionary transformation can require breaking with inherited moral conventions.
Overcoming fixed divisions supports entry into nontraditional social roles.
Revolutionary change need not wait for gradual institutional adjustment.
Social education should explain real relations, while exact modern identity curricula remain a contingent choice.
Connection to the past is insufficient to require maintaining obsolete customs.

axes.brief: Productive development can enable emancipation; SEP documents competing productivist and ecological readings rather than an automatic technology-at-any-cost stance.
axes.counterEvidence: Anachronistic AI, implants and gene editing are assessed conditionally through emancipation, safety and material development; no quotations or precise historical predictions are invented.

answers.rationale: Productive development matters but effects on human flourishing must be judged socially.
Universal delay and unrestricted deployment both exceed a context-sensitive material assessment.
Productive infrastructure can justify limited habitat loss while ecological reproduction still matters.
Protection of workers and common health supports meaningful safety evidence.
Labour-saving AI can liberate time or intensify exploitation depending on social control.
Preservation does not automatically outweigh necessary material development.
Novel food could improve production but ecological effects require evidence.
Irreversible nontherapeutic intervention warrants substantial scientific evidence.
Technical progress and changed production-consumption relations are complementary.
Scientific assessment should precede poorly understood irreversible projects.
Individual development supports enhancement while material risk qualifies premature use.
Shared health requires reliable evidence across populations.
Expanding human capacities and resisting instrumentalisation give a conditional enhancement judgement.
Scientific cultivation should assess ecosystem effects before wide release.
Meeting collective housing and transport needs can justify developing land.
Avoidable irreversible harm undermines the productive and human basis of emancipation.

axes.brief: The Commune combines local producer self-government with important national functions and an explicit rejection of breaking national unity.
axes.counterEvidence: Manifesto centralisation and Commune local accountability coexist. The later concrete communal account qualifies an uncomplicated central-state reading.

answers.rationale: The Commune protects producer self-government.
National functions should be exercised by accountable delegates, not automatic supremacy.
The Commune affirms national unity while opposing domination; a universal secession rule does not follow.
National plans need coordination but must not recreate an independent bureaucratic ruler.
Communal constitutions can embody local democratic self-government.
The Commune explicitly removes police from central-government political command.
Common social production requires resources beyond wealthy local areas.
Free public education and local control constrain automatic national curriculum command.
Local fiscal administration is compatible with common redistributive duties.
Workers need broadly applicable protections against competitive exploitation.
Local communal organisation should be responsive to its members.
Common health provision supports nationally coordinated entitlements.
Producer and community self-government supports Indigenous local administration as an inference.
National solidarity can constrain local competition to attract capital.
Locally confined land management belongs substantially to communal administration.
Important national coordination is explicitly retained for common tasks.

axes.brief: Theses VI–VII and historical materialism stress social relations; Gotha explicitly recognises unequal physical and mental endowments.
axes.counterEvidence: No genetic percentages follow from historical materialism. Recognised natural endowments justify mixed answers on individual cognition while social explanations dominate institutional and racial hierarchy claims.

answers.rationale: Social relations and practical activity strongly shape human conduct.
Historical materialism stresses social development while Gotha recognises differing natural endowments; together these do not fix the causal majority behind present-day country IQ differences.
Historical division of labour gives a strong social explanation of gender behaviour.
Gotha recognises bodily differences while material conditions shape stress exposure.
Productive activity and opportunities shape interests and realised capacities.
Natural endowments and learned material circumstances both affect risk-taking.
Changing social relations is expected to cultivate cooperative conduct.
Social development of concern coexists with differing individual capacities.
Educational conditions matter without denying unequal cognitive endowments.
The Manifesto relates moral consciousness to historical social conditions.
Historically formed social relations shape perceived threats.
Recognised individual endowments qualify a purely social explanation of temperament.
Embodied needs and historically changing ideals both shape attraction.
Class and social conditions weigh against inherited racial explanations of violence.
Praxis and upbringing challenge a fixed racial account of self-control.

The historical organisation of production and household labour supplies a structural explanation of earnings differences, rather than treating sex differences in productive contribution as the principal cause.

review.notes: Read all 240 answers against the current question wording and checked values, rationales, cited source IDs and axis distinctions. Checked Manifesto, Commune, Gotha and Engels against SEP/IEP distinctions between transition and higher-phase communism. Corrected Nationalism15: international association does not mean agreement with retaining national control, and the texts do not prescribe an unconditional political-federation rule. Preserved elected recallable Commune institutions and national coordination. Tightened the country-IQ inference; pay-gap explanation concerns historically organised work rather than moral worth. All answers remain labelled inferred: these are scoped representative models, not claimed questionnaire responses or empirical measurements of adherents. Review used no target scores or similarity tuning. Similarity audit remains the catalogue coordinator’s separate step.
